title: Wegwagonock
summary: Wegwagonock was once a large settlement in what is now the northern shore of Sag Harbor town. In around 1846, the ground containing burials and evidence of a Native village site were destroyed and used as stability material for the ship and oil yards.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: In the mid-nineteenth century, the ancestral burials and archaeological remains of the Wegwagonock settlement in Sag Harbor were tragically destroyed to provide stability material for booming commercial ship and oil yards. Remembering the physical erasure of this thriving coastal village underscores the devastating cultural costs of rapid industrial development, highlighting the urgent need to protect remaining Indigenous heritage sites today.
history_content: 1896, 1911. The location of Wegwagonock was reconstructed through East Hampton land-purchase records from the 1700s and placed in the Sag Harbor area. Older descriptions connected the name with a swamp, watercourse, and spring on the west side of Sag Harbor, near land later associated with the East Hampton Branch Railroad. The exact bounds remain uncertain, but the name preserves a Sag Harbor-area Native placename and wetland context.
vandalism_content:
William Wallace Tooker describes the destruction of Wegwagonock in 1896;

A large portion of the elevation, on the southern slopes of which the most compact part of the village had been situated, was leveled about 50 years ago [ca 1846, today's Bay Street waterfront.] and its contents distributed over the adjoining meadow in order to increase the area and stability of the ship and oil yards of Mulford and Sleight. The writer was informed by William R. Sleight that human bones, supposed to have been bones of Indians, very frail and decayed, were unearthed during the excavating; but if any object aboriginal were deposited with them at the time of burial, they were overlooked in the haste of carelessness of the digging.
